passage:
First week of October. Yamini found out from a photo: the five of them at the lake cafe, at the table she always sat at, with a caption about "the real ones". Nobody had told her. She sat on her hostel bed and let herself cry, then typed in her notes: "This hurts. It doesn't mean I'm unlovable."
Two weeks later. She messaged Ramesh from her lab group, the quiet one who always shared his charger: "Want to grab chai after practicals?" They talked about mosquitoes and question papers for an hour. She joined the Sunday cycling club too.
November. Someone from the old group posted about a party she wasn't invited to. Her thumb hovered over "leave group", then over a sharp reply. She did neither. She muted it and texted Ramesh about Sunday's ride.

qa.q: What did Yamini type in her notes?
qa.a: "This hurts. It doesn't mean I'm unlovable."

qa.q: What does Yamini's thumb hovering over a sharp reply suggest she was feeling in November?
qa.a: She still felt the sting and some urge to hit back, even after building new friendships.

qa.q: Which choice in November showed Yamini's recovery?
qa.a: She neither left angrily nor replied sharply; she muted the group and turned to Ramesh and the Sunday ride instead.

qa.q: How might Ramesh experience Yamini's invitation for chai?
qa.a: Ramesh, the quiet one in the lab group, may feel pleasantly noticed, so the new friendship matters to him too.

grounding: Over two months a young adult cut out of a friend group admits the hurt, builds new connections and resists striking back.

passage: Parul, beta, you think nobody has ever been dropped by their friends? When your Vasudha maasi was twenty-one, my whole group at the teachers' training college stopped calling me. One day I was sharing their lunch; the next day they had a new table and no seat for me. I never found out why. For weeks I thought something must be broken in me. Then one night I told myself: this hurts, and it is allowed to hurt, but it does not make me bad. I started eating with the two quiet girls from the science section, Farida and Rose. We are still friends; Rose sends me mangoes every summer. When one of the old group later came to me for notes, I gave them. I didn't want to become the thing that had hurt me. So cry today, beta. Tomorrow, find your Roses.

qa.q: What does Rose send Vasudha maasi every summer?
qa.a: Rose sends her mangoes every summer.

qa.q: What did young Vasudha believe about herself in the first weeks, and what changed?
qa.a: She thought something must be broken in her, until she told herself the hurt was allowed but did not make her bad.

qa.q: Why did giving notes to someone from the old group matter to Vasudha maasi?
qa.a: It was a choice not to shut someone out in return, so she wouldn't become the thing that had hurt her.

qa.q: What might Parul take from "find your Roses"?
qa.a: Parul might see that today's pain is real but that new, accepting friends can be found, as Vasudha maasi found Farida and Rose.

grounding: An elder recalls being dropped by her college group, admitting the hurt, finding new friends and refusing to exclude in return.

passage: The rain had knocked out the PG's power for the third night, and Jyoti was revising for her final exam by phone torch when she saw it: her four roommates had made a new chat for the farewell trip, and she wasn't in it. The kettle was dead, her battery was at twelve percent, and the exam was at nine. She let herself feel it for a minute, face in the pillow. Then she typed to her mother: "Feeling left out today. I'm okay, just sad." Her mother replied, "Call me after the exam." Next she messaged Rehana from her tutorial class: "Revising Paper 6? Library tomorrow after the exam?" Rehana said yes. Jyoti thought about sending her roommates a cold "enjoy your trip". She didn't. She plugged in the power bank and opened her notes.

qa.q: What was Jyoti's phone battery at when she saw the new chat?
qa.a: Her battery was at twelve percent.

qa.q: What does "Feeling left out today. I'm okay, just sad" show about how Jyoti is handling it?
qa.a: She admits the hurt honestly without deciding it means something is wrong with her.

qa.q: What choice did Jyoti make about the "enjoy your trip" message, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She didn't send it; striking back would have fed the coldness, while messaging Rehana and her mother gave her real support.

qa.q: How might Rehana experience the library invitation?
qa.a: Rehana might simply see a classmate wanting a study partner, and a new friendship could grow from it without any backstory.

grounding: On a hard night before an exam, a young adult left out by roommates admits the hurt, reaches out to others and does not retaliate.

passage: Avni, twenty, found out on a Sunday morning: her four closest college friends had gone to a birthday dinner in Koregaon Park, and she hadn't been invited. The photos were everywhere. She sat on the edge of her bed and let herself cry. "This hurts," she wrote in her journal. "It doesn't mean I'm broken." That week she messaged Manoj from her NSS unit, who always saved her a seat at the tree-planting drives. "Chai after the drive on Saturday?" He replied with a thumbs-up. They talked for two hours about their villages and bad hostel food. She joined his Sunday reading group too. When one of the old group asked her for notes later, Avni thought about saying no, as they had to her. She sent them anyway.

qa.q: Where did Avni's friends go for the birthday dinner?
qa.a: They went to a birthday dinner in Koregaon Park.

qa.q: How did Avni feel when she found out, and how did she see herself?
qa.a: She was deeply hurt and cried, but told herself the hurt did not mean she was broken.

qa.q: What choice did Avni make when her old friend asked for notes, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She sent the notes anyway instead of excluding them back, which kept her from becoming like the people who hurt her.

qa.q: How might Manoj see Avni's message about chai?
qa.a: Manoj would likely be pleased to be asked, since he already saved her a seat, and glad to spend time with her.

grounding: A young woman excluded by her friend circle admits the hurt, reaches out to others, and chooses not to retaliate with exclusion.

passage:
"You've been staring at that phone for an hour, Vinita." Zeenat sat down on the other bed in their hostel room.
"They made a new group for the Goa trip. I'm not in it."
"The four from your class?"
"Yes." Vinita's voice cracked. "I thought we were close."
Zeenat put an arm round her.
"That really hurts."
"It does. And I keep thinking, what's wrong with me?"
"Nothing's wrong with you. Maybe something changed with them. That's not the same thing."
Vinita wiped her eyes. "My birthday's next week. I could just not invite them either."
"You could. Would it make you feel better?"
Vinita thought. "No. It would make me like them."
"Come to my theatre group rehearsal tomorrow. They're a mad bunch, you'll like them."
"Okay." Vinita put the phone face down. "And I'll invite who I want, not who I'm angry at."

qa.q: What trip was the new group made for?
qa.a: The new group was made for the Goa trip.

qa.q: What was Vinita worried about when she said 'what's wrong with me'?
qa.a: She was worried that being left out meant there was something wrong with her.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vinita's thinking?
qa.a: When Zeenat asked if not inviting them would help, Vinita realised it would only make her like them, and chose not to retaliate.

qa.q: How does Zeenat see Vinita's hurt?
qa.a: Zeenat takes it seriously, telling her it really hurts and nothing is wrong with her, and offers a new group to join.

grounding: A young woman excluded from a friend circle admits the hurt, refuses to blame herself or retaliate, and reaches out to new people.

passage: In second year, Dilnaz's group stopped inviting me. There was no fight. Just one weekend they all went to Lonavala, and I saw the photos. Then another. By Diwali, I was out of their group chat. It hurt more than I'd admit. For a while I lay in my hostel bed thinking something must be wrong with me: too loud, too boring, too something. Then my roommate said, "Hafsa, you've been sad for weeks. Come to badminton." I went. I also started eating with the girls from my lab. I told my old school friend, on the phone, how much it had hurt, and just saying it helped. When Dilnaz later messaged about notes, I was tempted to ignore her the way they'd ignored me. I didn't. I sent the notes. I just didn't try to get back in. I'm Hafsa, and I'm okay now.

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz's group go one weekend?
qa.a: They all went to Lonavala.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel after being dropped from the group chat?
qa.a: Hafsa felt hurt and began to doubt, wondering whether something was wrong with Hafsa.

qa.q: Which of Hafsa's choices helped recovery, and why?
qa.a: Admitting the hurt, reaching out to new people like the lab group and badminton, and not retaliating let Hafsa rebuild without deciding something was wrong inside.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt when Hafsa sent the notes?
qa.a: Dilnaz might have felt relieved and perhaps a little guilty, receiving kindness after shutting Hafsa out.

grounding: A young adult excluded from a friend circle admits the hurt, reaches out to others and avoids retaliating, recovering without deciding the fault lies within.

passage:
Hostel counsellor's note, Thursday.
Shankar (second-year) came in today. His old friend circle from first year has started excluding him: plans made without him, a trip he learned about from photos. He said he felt "like a door slammed." He also said, "Maybe I'm just annoying." We talked about how exclusion hurts like real pain, and that it doesn't prove anything is wrong with him. He's already started going to the photography club and has two new friends there. He admitted he'd thought about posting a photo from a party they weren't invited to, "to show them." He decided not to. He wants to stay polite with the old group without chasing them. I suggested he keep in touch with his school friends too. We'll meet in two weeks.
- Shalini, counsellor

qa.q: How did Shankar learn about the trip?
qa.a: He learned about it from photos.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling when he said "like a door slammed"?
qa.a: Shankar felt hurt and shut out, and began to doubt himself, wondering if he was annoying.

qa.q: Which of Shankar's choices help him recover?
qa.a: Admitting the hurt, joining the photography club, choosing not to post a revenge photo and staying polite without chasing the old group.

qa.q: How might the counsellor see Shankar's progress?
qa.a: The counsellor seems encouraged, seeing him reach out to others and resist retaliating.

grounding: A young adult excluded by his friend circle admits the hurt, reaches out to new people, and resists retaliating or blaming himself.

passage:
Saturday night
Ganga's group went to the café again tonight. I saw it on stories. Fourth time this month without me. Nobody said why. I cried in the shower, then felt stupid for crying.
But I'm trying something. First, I'm writing down that it hurts. It does. It really does.
Second, I called Tanvi from my old school. We talked for an hour and she said she'd missed me.
Third, I said yes when the girl in my lab asked if I wanted to join their study group on Monday.
I keep hearing a voice saying, "You're the problem." I'm choosing not to believe it. People drift. It happens.
I thought about making my own group and not inviting Ganga. That would feel good for five minutes. I'm not doing it.
- Avni

qa.q: How many times this month had Ganga's group gone without Avni?
qa.a: It was the fourth time this month.

qa.q: How does Avni feel about being left out?
qa.a: Avni feels hurt and a little foolish for crying, but is determined not to believe the voice saying Avni is the problem.

qa.q: Which of Avni's steps are healthy ways to recover?
qa.a: Admitting the hurt, calling an old friend, joining a new study group, and deciding not to exclude Ganga in return.

qa.q: How might Tanvi have felt getting Avni's call?
qa.a: Tanvi seemed happy and warm, saying she'd missed Avni.

grounding: A young adult excluded by a friend circle admits the hurt, reaches out to others, refuses self-blame and avoids retaliating with exclusion.

passage:
In the small college town of Hazaribagh, Arnab's circle of four friends had stopped saving him a seat at the tea stall. He found out from a photo that they'd gone to the waterfall without him.
For two days he stayed in his room. Maybe I'm boring, he thought. Maybe I talk too much.
On the third day he told Thomas, from his lab, "I'm feeling a bit left out lately." Thomas said, "Come to the chess club on Friday. We're a strange lot, you'll fit."
Arnab went. He lost every game and laughed a lot.
He still nodded at the old group in the corridor. He didn't gossip about them or try to turn anyone against them.

qa.q: Where did the circle of friends go without Arnab?
qa.a: They went to the waterfall without him.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling during the two days in his room?
qa.a: He felt hurt and doubted himself, wondering if he was boring or talked too much.

qa.q: What choices helped Arnab recover?
qa.a: He admitted the hurt to Thomas, joined the chess club, and didn't retaliate against the old group.

qa.q: How might Thomas see Arnab joining the chess club?
qa.a: Thomas probably feels glad to welcome him, seeing him as a fun new member rather than someone rejected.

grounding: Shows a young adult shut out of a friend circle admitting the hurt, reaching out to new people and not retaliating.

passage:
In her second year at university in Toronto, Yuki's study group quietly stopped inviting her. She saw them in the library, laughing at a table, the one she used to sit at.
That night she wrote in her notebook: I feel stupid and hurt. Then, under it: This doesn't mean I'm unlikeable. Groups change.
The next week she sat next to Jamal in statistics, who always seemed to study alone. "Want to compare notes before the quiz?"
He smiled. "I'd love that."
When one of her old group asked, a month later, if she wanted to join their study session, she said, "Maybe another time," without any bitterness. She meant it.

qa.q: What did Yuki write under "I feel stupid and hurt"?
qa.a: She wrote: This doesn't mean I'm unlikeable. Groups change.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling when she saw the group laughing in the library?
qa.a: She felt hurt and left out, seeing them at the table she used to sit at.

qa.q: What helped Yuki move on in a healthy way?
qa.a: Admitting the hurt in writing, reminding herself it wasn't a flaw in her, and reaching out to Jamal instead of retaliating.

qa.q: How might Jamal feel when Yuki sits next to him?
qa.a: Jamal likely feels pleased and welcomed, since he usually studied alone.

grounding: Shows a young adult shut out of a study group admitting the hurt, not concluding something is wrong with her, and making new connections without retaliating.

passage: The counselling room at the university was warm and smelled of tea. Ira kept her jacket on. "My old group made a new chat without me," she said. "I saw the photos from the trip." Her voice wobbled. "It hurts more than I expected." The counsellor waited. "Part of me wants to post my own photos and not invite them to anything." "And the other part?" "The other part knows that's what they did." Ira looked at her hands. "My lab partner, Sachin, asked me to the film club twice. I said no both times." "What if you said yes this week?" Ira nodded slowly. That Friday she went. She laughed twice. It still hurt. But she didn't think something was wrong with her.

qa.q: What did Ira see from the old group?
qa.a: The photos from the trip.

qa.q: How did Ira feel about being left out?
qa.a: She felt deeply hurt, and also tempted to get back at them by excluding them in return.

qa.q: What helped Ira most, and why?
qa.a: Saying yes to Sachin's invitation to the film club, because it connected her with people who wanted her there.

qa.q: What might Sachin think when Ira finally comes to the film club?
qa.a: He might feel pleased that she finally accepted, not knowing how hard the week had been for her.

grounding: Shows a young adult excluded from a friend circle admitting the hurt, reaching out to others and not retaliating.

passage:
Dear Simran,
It's been ages. I'm writing because you once told me honesty works better than pretending. So here it is. The friends I made in first year have drifted into a new circle, and I'm not in it. I found out when I saw a birthday dinner I didn't know about. I sulked for a week. I drafted a sarcastic message and deleted it. I thought about not inviting any of them to my birthday. I won't. That's their way, not mine. I've started having tea with two people from my department instead, and last Sunday I called Mummy and admitted it hurt. I'm okay. I'm not broken. I just miss being known, so I'm writing to someone who knows me.
Nitin

qa.q: How did Nitin find out about the new circle?
qa.a: By seeing a birthday dinner Nitin didn't know about.

qa.q: What does "I'm not broken" suggest about how Nitin feels?
qa.a: It suggests Nitin still feels hurt and lonely but has decided the exclusion does not mean something is wrong with Nitin.

qa.q: Which choices in the letter helped Nitin cope?
qa.a: Admitting the hurt to Mummy, deleting the sarcastic message, not retaliating, and reaching out to new people and to Simran.

qa.q: How might Simran feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Simran might feel touched and trusted, glad to be the one Nitin turned to.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult shut out of a circle who admits the hurt, reaches out elsewhere and refuses to retaliate.

passage: Rashmi, you asked why I stopped mentioning the flat girls. Honestly? They planned the whole Goa trip in a chat without me. I only found out from the tickets on the table. I cried in the bathroom. Then I got angry. I wanted to plan something with the others in class and pointedly not ask them. I even started the chat. Then I deleted it. It would have been me doing the same thing. So I did the boring stuff instead. I told one of them, calmly, that it hurt. She said sorry, sort of. I started going to the running group on Sundays. I call you more, as you've noticed. I'm fine. Some days are hard. That's all it is. I'm Ritu, not some leftover.

qa.q: How did Ritu find out about the Goa trip?
qa.a: From the tickets on the table.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling after finding out?
qa.a: Ritu felt deeply hurt, crying in the bathroom, then angry enough to want revenge by excluding them.

qa.q: What choice did Ritu make instead of retaliating, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Ritu deleted the revenge chat, calmly told one flatmate it hurt, and joined the running group, keeping self-respect without hurting others.

qa.q: How might Rashmi see Ritu's recent calls?
qa.a: Rashmi noticed Ritu calling more and may feel glad to be trusted and supportive in a hard time.

grounding: Shows a young adult shut out by flatmates admitting the hurt, reaching out and avoiding revenge exclusion.

passage: I'm Jahnavi, Vinita's roommate in second year, so I saw most of it. In October her old gang from first year made a new group and simply left her out: the trips, the birthday dinners, all of it turned up in photos she wasn't in. For a few nights she was very quiet, and once I heard her crying on a call with her sister. I don't know everything she felt. But she told me plainly, "It hurts, and I don't know what I did." She didn't post anything nasty. She didn't start a rival group. Instead she joined the Sunday trekking club, started eating dinner with the girls from the third floor, and kept texting the two old friends who still replied. By December she was laughing again. Once she said, "Maybe we just grew apart. It doesn't mean I'm the problem."

qa.q: Which club did Vinita join?
qa.a: The Sunday trekking club.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi think Vinita felt, and why?
qa.a: Vinita was very quiet for nights, cried on a call with her sister and said plainly that it hurt, though Jahnavi cannot know everything she felt.

qa.q: Which of Vinita's choices helped her recover?
qa.a: Admitting the hurt, joining the trekking club, making new dinner friends and staying in touch with those who replied, while refusing to retaliate.

qa.q: How might the old gang see Vinita now?
qa.a: They may barely notice, or be surprised she moved on without bitterness, since she never posted anything nasty or formed a rival group.

grounding: A roommate watches a young woman shut out by her old friends admit the hurt, find new people and refuse to exclude anyone in return.
